name: Cetyl tranexamate mesylate

lead: Cetyl tranexamate mesylate is a modified form of tranexamic acid made for skincare. People use it in serums aimed at dark spots, uneven tone and post-acne marks.

Tranexamic acid is thought to reduce the signalling that drives melanocyte pigment production, and the cetyl chain makes the molecule more fat-soluble so it can cross the skin barrier better than the parent compound. A 2021 study in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology examined its skin-lightening performance on sun-damaged skin, and a small registered trial looked at acne-related hyperpigmentation.

paras: It is applied as a leave-on serum or cream, usually daily and often with sunscreen, since sun exposure drives pigmentation. It is commonly combined with other brightening ingredients. Fading of marks is judged over weeks to months.
Sources reviewed report no specific safety concerns, but long-term data are lacking. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient; as with any topical, irritation is possible.

angle.text: Cetyl tranexamate mesylate is a fat-soluble tranexamic acid form used in serums to reduce pigment production, so dark spots fade and tone looks more even. Published data include a 2021 cosmetic-dermatology study and a small registered trial.

lead: Cetyl tranexamate mesylate is a lipophilic derivative of tranexamic acid, formulated as a cosmetic ingredient for topical skin-lightening and hyperpigmentation products. It is the cetyl ester of tranexamic acid supplied as a mesylate salt.[1][2]

Tranexamic acid itself is a hydrophilic zwitterionic molecule that is described as penetrating the stratum corneum poorly; formulators have used penetration enhancers, microneedling or lipophilic derivatives such as cetyl tranexamate mesylate to address this.[2] The derivative is marketed for uneven skin tone and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

Published evidence is limited. A 2021 study in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology examined its safety and skin-lightening performance on sun-damaged skin,[1] and a small registered trial examined its effect on acne-related hyperpigmentation.[3]

paras: It is used in leave-on serums and creams aimed at dark spots, melasma-like discoloration and post-acne marks. The rationale is that attaching a cetyl (long fatty) chain makes the molecule more lipophilic than tranexamic acid, which may improve delivery through the skin barrier.[2]

Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic; its proposed skin-lightening action involves reducing plasmin-related signalling that stimulates melanocytes. The cetyl ester is presented as a topical delivery form of this approach. Detailed pharmacokinetic data for the derivative are not available in the sources reviewed.

A 2021 report in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology investigated the safety and skin-lightening performance of cetyl tranexamate mesylate in sun-damaged skin, framing it as a new topical bioactive for hyperpigmentation and inflammation.[1] A separate registered study (NCT06080035), completed with 22 participants and started in November 2023, examined effects on the appearance of acne-related post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation; it is listed as a non-randomised (NA phase) study.[3] Larger independent randomised trials have not been identified. For the parent compound, a general reference notes that efficacy for melasma remained unproven as of 2017, with no large randomised trials.[2]
